young.html: Geoffrey Chaucer lived in London about 650 years ago and is often called the father of English poetry. He wrote in the English of his day, called Middle English. It looks strange to us, but if you read it out loud, you can understand more than you expect.

Troilus and Criseyde is a long poem set during the war at Troy, the same war Homer wrote about. Troilus is a young prince of Troy. He loves Criseyde, and with the help of his friend Pandarus they promise to be true to each other. But then Criseyde is sent away to the Greek camp, and she does not keep her promise to come back. It is a sad story about trust, friendship and change.

People in Chaucer's time liked to picture life as a great wheel turned by a lady called Fortune. Sometimes you ride up to the top; then the wheel turns and down you go. Troilus rides the wheel all the way up and all the way down.

young.html: Decode Middle English. Read these lines out loud, slowly: "The double sorwe of Troilus to tellen, / That was the king Priamus sone of Troye." Sorwe sounds like sorrow; sone like son. What do the lines mean? (The double sorrow of Troilus to tell, who was King Priam's son, of Troy.) Now try: "Fro wo to wele, and after out of Ioye." The letter I here stands for J.
For parents: this is a grown-up love story. The lesson keeps to the plot and the big ideas, Fortune and faithfulness; the poem's love scenes are better for older readers.

full.html: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) was the son of a London wine merchant. He served kings as a page, soldier, diplomat and customs official, and traveled to Italy on royal business in the 1370s, where he came to know the works of Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio. He wrote Troilus and Criseyde in the 1380s, before the Canterbury Tales. It is his longest finished poem, about 8,200 lines in five books.

The story is not in Homer. It grew up in the Middle Ages, in a French poem of the 1100s about Troy, and was retold by Boccaccio in Italian as Il Filostrato. Chaucer used Boccaccio closely but made the story deeper and slower, and gave much more life to Criseyde and to Pandarus. He pretends, playfully, to be translating an old writer he calls "Lollius," who did not exist.

full.text:
The double sorwe of Troilus to tellen,
That was the king Priamus sone of Troye,
In lovinge, how his aventures fellen
Fro wo to wele, and after out of Ioye,
My purpos is, er that I parte fro ye.
Thesiphone, thou help me for tendyte
Thise woful vers, that wepen as I wryte!
full.work: Troilus and Criseyde, Book I, lines 1 to 7
full.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
full.note: Glosses: sorwe, sorrow; aventures fellen, fortunes went; wo to wele, woe to happiness; Ioye, joy; er, before; Thesiphone, one of the Furies; tendyte, to write.

full.html: Chaucer wrote the poem in seven-line stanzas rhyming ABABBCC, with ten-syllable lines. The form was later called rhyme royal. It is long enough to tell a bit of story and ends with a rhyming couplet that can sum up or turn it.

full.html: The plot is simple; the poem is long because Chaucer lets us into his characters' minds. Troilus, who laughed at lovers, falls in love and is helpless. Pandarus is a talkative, clever friend and matchmaker, full of proverbs. Criseyde is thoughtful and cautious, a widow alone in a city at war, whose father, the prophet Calchas, has gone over to the Greeks. When the Trojans trade her to the Greek camp, she means to return; but she is frightened and alone, and in the end she accepts the Greek Diomede.

Chaucer, as narrator, refuses to condemn her harshly. He says he would excuse her if he could, for she was so sorry for what she did. Readers have argued ever since whether Criseyde is faithless, or a person caught by Fortune and fear.
In the opening of Book II, Chaucer asks his readers not to laugh at the old-fashioned ways of lovers in his story. Language and customs change, he says, and that is natural.

full.text:
Ye knowe eek, that in forme of speche is chaunge
With-inne a thousand yeer, and wordes tho
That hadden prys, now wonder nyce and straunge
Us thinketh hem; and yet they spake hem so,
And spedde as wel in love as men now do;
Eek for to winne love in sondry ages,
In sondry londes, sondry ben usages.
full.work: Troilus and Criseyde, Book II, lines 22 to 28
full.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
full.note: Glosses: eek, also; tho, then; hadden prys, were valued; wonder nyce, very foolish; spedde, succeeded; sondry, different; usages, customs.

full.html: Chaucer's point is truer than he could know: his own English now needs glosses. Over about 650 years, the sounds of English vowels shifted (the "Great Vowel Shift"), many endings dropped away, and thousands of words changed meaning.

Chaucer translated Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, a Roman book written in prison about Fortune, fate and God's knowledge, and its ideas run all through Troilus. In Book IV, Troilus, alone in a temple, argues at length that everything must happen as God foresees it, so he cannot be free. Boethius had answered that argument; Troilus, in his grief, does not hear the answer.

Thinking the poem simply blames Criseyde. Chaucer shows a world where people want to be faithful but are moved by fear, chance and pressure. He asks us to see how hard faithfulness is, and also how much it matters.

deep.html: After Troilus is killed in battle, his spirit rises to the eighth sphere of heaven. From there he looks down at the little Earth and laughs at the grief of those weeping for him, seeing how small earthly troubles are beside heaven. Chaucer then turns to his young readers, urging them to love God, who will never betray anyone who trusts him. He sends the poem off ("Go, little book") and asks his friends, the poet John Gower and the philosopher Ralph Strode, to correct it.
Readers argue about this ending. Does it reject the love story, crown it, or set it in a larger frame? The same view from the heavens appears in Dante's Paradiso, which Chaucer knew.

The Scottish poet Robert Henryson wrote a sequel, and Shakespeare's darker play Troilus and Cressida (later on this ladder) retold the story again. "Pandar," from Pandarus, even became an English word, though Chaucer's Pandarus is a warmer friend than the word suggests.

items: Is Criseyde to blame, or Fortune, or the war? Can it be all three?
Troilus thinks that if God knows the future, we are not free. How might Boethius or Aquinas answer him?
Why does Chaucer end a love story by looking down from the stars?
Chaucer says that ways of speaking change in a thousand years. What words of ours might sound strange in the year 3000?

deep.html: Compare Homer's Iliad for the war, Dante for the heavens, and Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida for a different telling.

questions: Have you ever made a promise that was very hard to keep? What made it hard?
Pandarus is a helpful friend, but is he always a good one? What makes a good friend?
Do you think Criseyde should be blamed? Why or why not?
Fortune's wheel goes up and down. Is life really like that? What stays the same when the wheel turns?
Read one Middle English line aloud together. Which words could you guess?
care: A story of grown-up romance. The lesson keeps to the plot and the ideas about Fortune, faithfulness and language, and quotes only the opening stanza and Chaucer's lines on how language changes.
